blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that this is Bill Russell interviewing Mr. Abby Foster, Chai Nee, the famous drummer. How you start off. Interviewing him for Barry Martin. We'll send this to Barry. I'm sorry Barry didn't get to talk to you. But I'll try to ask you a few questions about your life and drumming. Do you want to start off giving your full name?
Yes, sir.
How did you get that name, Chai Nee, too?

You see, when I first started, as I told you once before, I was a little kid. I'll be 61 on the 19th of March, St. Joseph Cummins. Born 1900, I'm with the year. Well, I got the name of Chai Nee by playing with white and colored bands. See, when I was a little boy, well, musicians wasn't like you are today. Musicians were very sketchy. They didn't have jukeboxes and different things like that. Well, when I was a little boy, I used to play with white and colored bands, as I told you. And so, half of them thought I was Mexican, half of them thought I was Spanish, half of them thought I was Puerto Rican, you see. Well, at that time, children used to have long hair and things like that, you see. And so, well, I started playing around the Latin Slager market with different bands, like I told you, white and colored. So they didn't know whether I was white or what I was colored. Some of them used to think I was Indian, just like Lorenzo Teo, the great clarinet player, like I told you. So they all started picking names and things like that. And so, one time I went on the show, and I done a Charni act. So from that on, white and colored started calling me Charni. A lot of people would say, well, how do you call him Charni? He goes, Charni, a gentleman is not dark like him. They say, well, he do that Charni act so good, so we just call him Charni. And from that time on, up until now, well, they've been calling me Charni. And very few know my right name.
You were born right here in New Orleans?
Right here in New Orleans, yes.
I think you told us the other time about what street it was, what part of town?
Right around here. In the French Quarter? In the French Quarter, yes. Born on St. Philip, between Burgundy and Dauphin.
Did your father play any music?
No, nobody in my family.
How come you took up drums so young?
Well, it's just a gift. Nobody taught me whatsoever.
Just picked it up. Where did you get your first set of drums?

My first set of drums, Maggie Garnier. There you saw in the Ivy Theater, Annette and Villery. Well, I used to throw out circles for her. I also played there with a white band. It was three pieces. Two white fellas and myself. Piano, clarinet, and drum.
Where was that theater?
Villery and Annette.
Villery and Annette, downtown.
Yes.
What is the name of it?
Ivy.
The Ivy.
Ivy.
Ivy.
I have a theater.
Who were the other players in the trio?
Well, one fellow was named Henry McCarty and the other fellow named Pete Lewis. What?
Yeah. Oh. So you were talking about that trio. Who else played in the trio?
Peter Lewis. He was clarinet player.
Fair enough.
And I had his wife followed, Andrew. He was a piano player and I was on the drum.
How old were you when you did this?
I was eight years old.
Eight years old.
And from then on, I saw the gun.
I know you told us sometime you'd sit up on those balconies in the back of the drum. They couldn't even see you.
They couldn't see me. That's right. See, I was so small. As you can see from my size now. Yeah. But they couldn't see me up on the balcony.
Could you reach the pedal all right with your...
Well, I had a special stool made. I couldn't sit on the chair because I was too small.
What kind of a drum outfit did you have when you started?
When I started, I had a leady.
A leady.
Yeah, a leady set of drums.
How big was the bass drum and the snare? What kind of a...
Fourteen by twenty-six bass drum and a three by fifteen snare drum.
Just a little flat snare drum.
Flat drum, yeah.
That have two... A double head on it?
Double head, yes.
You were talking about this old Haitian drum that I have that has a single head. What kind of drums were those when they... You mentioned Mac Murray and who else?
John Veen.
John Veen had them.
I was back here around in 1910, 1908.
Somebody told me that Mac Murray used one that was made out of a banjo head. Do you know if it was really a banjo head or a special drum?
Well, that I couldn't say. But I know it only had one head to it.
Yeah. Were the snares right up underneath the head against it? Right up underneath the head, yeah.
Underneath the head.
Underneath the head.
But they were not made out of steel.
Mm-hmm.
They were cat guts here. Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
They wasn't making steel head snares at that time.
Did they have the regular little rods on to tighten it, you know, with the little brackets to tighten it? Yeah, they had the brackets. Yeah.
But there wasn't flathead keys.
Yeah.
They used to tighten those with the keys. The keys were not made like the keys on the drums of the day.
Yeah.

See, those keys was made different. They were made on the order, but not the same thing. Because those keys that they had at that time, you could open a water faucet with them. They were all together. They were much larger.
Yeah.
But they were made on the order, but they were much larger.
Mm-hmm. Did you ever have one of the drums that you had to tighten with a rope, you know? Yeah, I had.
That's what the drum I had, my 14 by 26, my first bass drum. The big bass drum. Yeah. They used to tighten rods, you know. I mean, the strings you pull the ears down on them.
Mm-hmm. What kind of... Traps? Oh, yeah. What kind of a foot pedal did you have?
We had a crow foot pedal.
One of the crow foot pedals.

They were made on the order, the flow pedals of today, but they were much larger, and they had wood balls on them. And we used to use the cymbal on the side of the drum. You know, the drum and the cymbal would beat together, just like they had an old-time electric piano.
Yes, I remember those out there.
Well, the foot pedal was made just on that order.
Yeah. Was that sort of an overhead pedal? Was it a string? No.
That come up... The overhead pedals come up behind that.
Yeah.
Came up behind that.
Yeah. What kind of cymbals did you use? That is, did you have a big... That's crash cymbal. Chinese...
Crash cymbal.
Crash cymbal. Did you have a Turkish cymbal, too, hanging up above?
No, we didn't use that at that time.
Just the one Chinese cymbal.
Just the one Chinese cymbal.
And then it was a smaller cymbal on the bass drum.

On the bass drum, yeah. That's why I tell you up today, I could take, not saying bragging on myself, but I could take an old style set of drums and make the same music that you make today with all the new style of tum-tum. You see, because at that time, what you done, you had to do it all with the bass drum and that cymbal on the side. Mm-hmm. So therefore, I could take, use the bass drum on the style I play, which they don't play up today.
Yeah.
I'd make as much on the bass drum as what you make with the full tum-tums that they add to the drums up today.
How many, did you have any tom-tums in those days?
They had tom-tums.
What kind did you have?
Had a little small Indian tom-tums. With the little nails around the head? Around, that's right.
That kind. Yeah. That would have a double head on it?
Double head, that's right.
Yeah.
Double head.
How big was that about?
Well, it was four by twelve.
About four by twelve. Yeah. Just one tom-tum?
Just one.
Just the one.
Just the one tom-tum and the crash cymbal.
Did you have any wood blocks?

Wood blocks, yeah. That was more famous. See, the wood block, at the time, when we were using wood blocks, well, if you're the play the bass drum, when you record a record at that time, it'd make a blow in the record. You wouldn't hear the other instruments.
Yeah.
So, therefore, at the time when we started making records at that time, well, quite natural, we used it, nothing but tum-tum, I mean, tum-tum and the wood block.
Yeah.
If you notice my last recording with Celestine and them, you remember while playing the whistle and playing the China block? Well, the drum wasn't taken at that time.
No, that's right. You didn't hear so much drum.
You heard the wood block.
Yeah.
Well, you see, that's what we used to make our time, time the band with that.
What kind of a slide whistle was that that you had? Do you remember how big it was?
Yes. Eleven minutes long.
Is it all metal just made out of the-
All metal.
Any special name or brand on it? Do you remember where you got it or anything?
Ludwig.
Ludwig. Ludwig. Ludwig. Ludwig.
Ludwig. Ludwig. Ludwig.
Harrison. Have a little wire on in your-
Made on all those trombones.
Yeah. Like trying to slide it back and forth.
Slide it backwards and forth.
Did anybody else in the band ever play that or did you always play that? No.
There wasn't but three that I know played those whistle.
Oh. Who else?
Lloyd Armstrong. Oh yeah.
He used it.
Red Happy and myself. Yeah.
Can you tell us anything about Red Happy's drumming? Anything about him? because I never got to hear him.

I tell you, he was a great drum player. Him and I used to fight all the time. It was a long time before they could find out who was the best, him or I. Well, quite naturally, they had friends of his and friends of mine. My friends would say I was the best. His friends would say he was the best. So I had come up. They had a telltale showdown at the Italian Hall. Espinade between Burgundy and Rampo. Well, he would play with Chris Kelly's band and I would play with Celestine. So it come down to a showdown. Well, so the musician voted for me and told him he's sorry, but I was the best. See, because when I had him best at, he was a kind of a bigoted fella. You see, and he wanted to play the way he wanted. I always had sense enough to play like the band wanted to play. Well, if they wanted to play and I didn't like it, I played it that way. Then every night, then I'd use my ideas in between. Well, it went on like that and went on like that, so come down to another showdown. He gave a kind, so he can give prizes. Love & Cuff, which I have the Love & Cuff at my house right now.
You still have it.
Well, I was about 80 to 20 over him.
How old was Red Happy? Was he older than you or younger?
Yeah, he was about two years old.

Two years old. Can you tell us anything about your early life when you started out, which other bands you played with? You mentioned that trio in the theater. Yes, sir. And then who else did you start to play?

Well, Robichaux. I played my, the first time I played in a band of music, I played with Robichaux up at St. Catherine Hall. I was making my community then. Well, Father Carter gave a concert for the school, to raise my funds for the school up there, Tulane Avenue across from the Charity Hospital.
Yes.

Well, that was in 1910. Well, during that time, well, I asked the fellas to let me play. So they said, I wasn't large enough and I didn't think I could fit in no band. So Father Carter asked them, well, if he break anything on the drum, that he would pay for him. He guaranteed that he would pay for him. So I happened to play one number. So after I played that number, it wasn't so good, they asked me to play it that way. And so from that on, that started me out. Well, the next way of them was Emmanuel Perez.
Who was the drummer with Robichaux?
A man by the name, wait, it's been so long now, all I can think of was John Brundy. John Brundy.
I heard of Walter Brundy.
Well, he's his brother.
That was his brother.
It was his brother.
And this is John Brundy.
John Brundy, yeah.
Remember who else was in the Robichaux band at that time?
Well, Andrew Kimball was playing bass, violin. I can't call his name right off the rear, but Robichaux, left-hand violin player.
Yeah.
Lady by the name of Miss Margaret was playing piano. And...
Trombone was?
Eddie Atkins. Eddie Atkins was playing trombone with him at the time. Charlie McQuarris was playing clarinet. That was his lineup.
And that was in 1910, then?
St. Catherine's Hall.
St. Catherine's Hall.
Then you... When did you... What was the next band you said you went with?
The next band I went with was Manuel Perez. They had a band named the Imperial Band.
Oh, yes. Yeah. Do you remember who else was in that band with Manuel?

In that band was Buddy Johnson trombone player. Manny Perez cornet player. They used the word trumpet at that time. Yeah. Cornet player. Mm-hmm. And... Alphonse Picou was playing clarinet. Oh, yeah. And Rene Baptiste was playing ghetto. Jimmy Brown playing bass. Mm-hmm. Played my first job with them up at the Lincoln Park.
Oh, yes. How old were you then? About still a little boy?

Yeah, I was a boy then. Mm-hmm. Well, quite naturally, just like I told you. You see, they would take up time with me because I was producing stuff that all the fellas wasn't producing then. You understand what I mean? Yeah. And then musicians were skates.
Yeah.
See, now, when I was playing with those fellas, as I first told you, when I started playing with them, I was doing relief work.
Yeah.
See, because my mother hadn't bought me no drums yet. See? Yeah. They didn't know what I was going to do. Mm-hmm. And in other words, they wasn't able to buy me no drums.
How did you learn so well with that? Did you get to practice on anybody's set?
I practiced, but I'd use a cheese box.
Yeah.
See, I'd make my own drum.
Yeah.
Cheese box. I'd make my drum get a little fallish there, blow the corn. They'd play the corn like a gazoo corn.
Yeah.
And we'd play together like that.
Did you have a good set of sticks or make your own sticks?
I made my sticks off of chairs. Chair. I made my drum sticks off of chairs. Mm-hmm.
After you learned to play, what kind of sticks did you use? Did you like heavy sticks or lightweight sticks or what kind of?
Lightweight sticks.
You always used lightweight sticks.
I always used lightweight sticks. Mm-hmm. Because I could do more with them. I couldn't handle them. Yeah. Yeah.
Any particular number or certain make that you used? Do you remember what kind of? Yeah.
Two A's.
The two A's?
Two A's.
Those Ludwig?
Ludwig sticks. Two A's, yeah.
Can you tell us anything else about your drum set, when you did get your drum set, anything about the snare drum, the way you would tune it or anything? How many?
Well, I tuned my snare drum up in there.
That was a, what make was it? A leadie, did you say?
Leadie.
Leadie.
Yeah, I used leadie and con. Mm-hmm. Well, because I got the same volume on all of it.
The con had a?
Had drums.
Had drums in those days. Had drums. You knew they had a music store here.
Yeah. Con's had drums in those days. Yeah. Say, the first one put out the nickel-plated drums.
Oh, yeah.
Con's was the first one. Put out the nickel-plated drums.
Your leadie, was it metal or wood?
Wood.
Wood.
Wood, yeah.
And you say you tuned it up to F?
To F.
To F. Uh-huh.
I tuned my snare drum up in F and tuned the bass drum up in D. To G? D. D. D, yeah.
Yeah, up to D. Is there anything else about your outfit that you can tell us? Anything like cowbells?
Cowbells, I used that myself. Yeah, I used that.
How many cowbells did you have?
Four.
Had a set of four.
Four cowbells, four china blocks.
Oh, yeah. Those sort of big red things that look like a dragon's mouth or something.
Dragon's mouth. Yeah, look like a coconut.
Yeah, coconut. Yeah. Sometimes they call them temple blocks.
Temple blocks. Well, that's the real name, temple blocks.
Temple blocks. Yeah.
But we so used to call them the single blocks, you know, the regular china blocks that we call them.
Yeah.
Two.
And you had a set of four of those.
Four of those.
Can you tell us? Can you tell us?
When I played those, I'd always watch myself.
Yeah.

See, that's a lot of things. Most one of the important things that drummers do not watch. See, I used them and called them. Called them, they'd say, well, according to what number the band were playing in. Well, I'd make sure I'd never hit those blocks unless I'm called with the instruments, with
the blowing instruments. Yeah, so they'd start to be in tune with them.
With the instruments. That's right. I didn't hit on them just to be hitting them. That's why I used to get the drummers.
Yeah.

I always make a style of my own. If a fella think I'm going to make one thing, I'd make something else, especially for drummers around me. Mm-hmm. See? He think I'm going to make one thing, I'll make something else. And I'd never make it the way he think I'm going to make it. See, if I make something one time, and I figure, fellas, after catching on to it, I'll make it a different way. I'll make it the opposite way.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

That's like right now, I have breaks that I can make, and I haven't heard nobody make them, not said myself, you know, to brag on myself. Yeah. But I haven't heard nobody make that kind of breaks and stuff since 1926, and you know, that's not today.
Yeah, that's right.
See, in making those breaks, and making drum solos, you must make that in time. Because if you don't make them in time, you're going to throw the band off.
Yeah, sure.

And you have to make it, and make it with a certain tempo, that you don't rush it, and you don't be behind. Mm-hmm. And never let your hand interfere with your feet. Your feet is your time. The hand is what you make your foolishness with.
Mm-hmm.

And otherwise, I can take my hand and play in 440, and they play in the waltz time, or or two beat time on the bass. Yeah. And they're playing 440 with my hand. Yeah. See, that's your time. Mm-hmm. See, that's your time. That's what you make your monkey shine with. Because I'd be watching my hand, and I'd be keeping time with the bass drum. They'd be trying to keep the time with the bass drum, but they had to be making it, so they threw the band off.
Yeah.

See, that's why you were talking. I said, if you be talking like that, I want to do something. I'll make boom. We're bummed. Yeah. I said, you see, but they never stopped the bass drum. Yeah. See, because that's your time.
Keep that going all the time.

And I was always taught by Mac Murray. He sat on. Well, he gave me the instruction about your time. See, like I once told you, I liked him for orchestra drummer, and I also liked it, Loie Contra for street drummer. So one day at the Lincoln Park, Mac Murray and I were talking, and he took nice liking and telling me because he saw that I was happening, he said, someday you'll make a great drummer. He said, well, I want to tell you one thing. He said, well, all you do, always watch your bass drum. He said, because that's the time you can make and you can break a band. It's not what your hands do, it's what your feet do. So always bear that in mind. Well, through talking, I paid attention and listened at what he was saying. And I come, I went home and I practiced it and I come to find out to be natural just like he told me. So I kept that on up and up until today. President Paul asked me, well, Chani, how you do such and such a thing? I said, oh, it's just a matter of knowing. Well, how'd you make it? Well, I said, well, I'll show them what I want them to know. Well, I'll never show them what I know. I'll show them what I want them to know.
Yeah. Did you ever take many drum solos in the old days, a whole chorus by yourself?
Yeah. I took many of them. That's what I was telling you about just now.
Yeah.

There's different ways that you can make it. You see, but plenty of fellas, they try to make it with their feet, but they make it with their hands, but they cannot do it. Because your hand is just a flesh. And your feet is your time.
What did you do? What did you think when you would be playing a drum solo? Did you sort of hum the melody to yourself? To myself.
To myself. Hum the melody to myself. That way you can't go wrong. Yeah.
You just didn't count it out like one, two, one, two, or up to 16 bars or something. You really hum the melody, sort of thought the melody to yourself.
That's to myself. And that way you can't go wrong.

No. I was wondering also about, speaking of the bass drum, in the old days did you use, nowadays you hear a lot of talk about four beat or two beat time. Did you ever think about whether you'd use four beats to the measure or two beats, or say in high society, how many beats with your bass drum would you do? One.
One.
If you're going to hum, could you hum in high society and start a beat with your foot, the shoulders, how often you beat? Yeah.

I had two pencils or something. In other words, here. In other words, to give you an idea of what I mean, that's the way you would do that. All right. . . . . See that? See those hands on the feet? Now I can talk with you all day and then it's still a whole long time.
That's it. Yeah, that's it.

And sometimes if you just want to change the beats, you're beating on one or two beats, but all you do, you make a break like this. Then you pick up on your four-poor. You're going out. Then you hit the whole line and you hit. Well, if I had the cymbals or something, I could hit. That's the way you make your breaks. Now, if you take it, you probably want to make a drum solo and that. Then you make... See, like nine, that's just enough to keep your hands in.
Yeah. That's that. Yeah. That's very interesting. It's the same as getting to hear you play, I don't know.

Yeah, well, you see, I don't have nothing, you know, that I can hit on that I can keep from breaking. Because it's a different style in the making, you see? You make it up a rap, you make it up a... Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. on the edge of my drum, I use the sticks this way.
See? One stick against the other. I have a set of sticks here someplace I can find.

You see, that's the way you make your brace. And there's different things. Never let your hands interfere with that. I have a set of sticks here. . . . The right way, the real way to play high society. You see, when the clarinet make this solo, well, you get off the drums like that. See what I mean?

Yes, yes. As I might describe how you're doing that, you're holding your sticks about the same as you always do. And you take your left hand and hit near the butt end, and sometimes of the right, and sometimes you hit up above your hand.

That's right. You hit on both. That's to make the stick change tone. If you notice, you notice your sticks are almost making notes. Yeah, that's right. So you got to know how to squeeze them to a certain extent to make them change the tone. Yeah. Now, you watch. Your left stick, they always hit right near the, between the tip and your hand. And the middle. Yeah.

And the middle. But your right hand stick, the right stick, sometimes hits the butt, and sometimes hits the butt, And the middle. Sometimes hits it. Sometimes hits it. Sometimes hits it. Sometimes hits it. Sometimes hits it. Yeah. Yeah. See? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It's the same way I make it all. Yeah. I've never seen that before. Mm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm-hm to have a way of hitting, holding both sticks in one hand, we call it nerve beats or something, shake them sort of like that, but I never saw anybody play it like you did there. Well that's the way Mac Murray did that.
Yeah, Mac Murray did that. See a lot of people use the edge of the bass though.
We don't use that. You'd hit on the stick in place of the, you know, I wish we had a movie of that, that's really something to see that too.
I'd like very much to demonstrate it to you too.

Someday maybe we can get a little camera and then make a movie of you doing that and some of the other things. It'd be wonderful. If you'd like to have those sticks, you can have them. Do they feel, are those pretty heavy or not? No, they're just right. Feel all right too. Because I have quite a few of those sticks. I think those are 5A, are they?
They're, yeah, 5A. 5A, I can't see what my glass is.
The make is HDC, I don't know, I think that's the Hall Drum Company. You know, the Hall Drum Company down here on Decatur Street. Decatur Street. They look like a...

Well, none of the drummers, those drummers never show you that. I tried to learn Alec Begaard that, but he never could learn it. I never saw anybody do that. Well, you know, in fact, to tell you the truth, Alec Begaard, our uncle was a great violin player too.
Oh yes, Emil.
Emil. Well, he was the first one that voted me over happy. Oh really? Yeah, and he was the one that made me know how good I was. We're just about out of tape here.
I'm going to need another reel of tape here. I'll get another one.
We've got plenty of time to talk.
Yeah.
And it's just anything that you come to your mind that you want to ask me, just ask me.

Oh, here's this pad if you want to make this chair a little softer. Here's another reel here. We'll... Any beat or anything? Did you have any special beats? I'll change this reel. And then that is of your, on your snare drum head. Just a second, I'll let this run out so we don't have... ... ... ... ...
I was wondering in the slow blues for instance if you had any special beats or what kind of a part you would play? Well the most anything that come in my mind, see now I've...

You just can't match any stuff. Now you take like this man up there. Now him and Joe Oliver's on the same style. Bunk Johnson. Bunk Johnson. Bunk Johnson and Joe Oliver, they're on the same style. Now you take Wallace, you take like Peter Bocas. Now he's a nice trumpet player. Mario Perez, Anorma Twier, Andrew Kimball. Those fellas, well they're more musical men. Sound like a reading music. That's it, and you see. Too much exercise. Well that's it.

segments.title: Opening: introducing Abby Foster for Barry Martyn
segments.summary: Russell announces the recording of drummer Abby 'Chinee' Foster and asks for his name and how he got the nickname.

segments.title: How he got the nickname Chinee
segments.summary: Foster explains that playing in white and colored bands as a long-haired boy, people took him for Mexican, Spanish or Indian, and a 'Chinee' act on a show gave him the name.

segments.title: Born in the French Quarter; no musical family
segments.summary: He was born on St. Philip Street in the French Quarter; nobody in his family played and nobody taught him drums.

segments.title: First drums and the Ivy Theater trio at age eight
segments.summary: At eight he played at the Ivy Theater with a white clarinetist and pianist, sitting on a special stool and hidden on the balcony because he was so small.

segments.title: His first drum outfit and early single-head drums
segments.summary: He describes his first set: 14x26 bass drum, double-head snare, and the single-head gut-snare drums of Mac Murray and John Veen, with rope or key tensioning.

segments.title: Foot pedal, cymbals and tom-tom of the early kit
segments.summary: He recalls the crow-foot pedal, the Chinese and side cymbals, and the single small tom-tom, and says he can still make modern effects on the old kit.

segments.title: Wood blocks, recording limits and the slide whistle
segments.summary: Bass drum caused blasts on early records so wood block was used for time; he describes his metal Ludwig slide whistle, played only by Lloyd Armstrong, Red Happy and himself.

segments.title: Rivalry with Red Happy and the drummers' showdowns
segments.summary: Foster tells of contests with Red Happy, who played with Chris Kelly, held at Italian Hall, where musicians voted him the better drummer and he won a loving cup.

segments.title: First band job with Robichaux at St. Catherine Hall
segments.summary: In 1910 Father Carter vouched for him to sit in with Robichaux's band at a school benefit; he names the lineup including John Brundy, Eddie Atkins and clarinetist McCurdy.

segments.title: Joining Manuel Perez's Imperial Band and relief work
segments.summary: His next band was Perez's Imperial Band with Buddy Johnson, Picou, Baptiste and Jimmy Brown; first job at Lincoln Park, doing relief work since he had no drums yet.

segments.title: Practicing on a cheese box and choice of sticks
segments.summary: He taught himself on a homemade cheese-box drum with chair-leg sticks and later preferred lightweight Ludwig 2A sticks.

segments.title: Snare drum make, Conn drums and tuning
segments.summary: He used Leedy and Conn drums, notes Conn made the first nickel-plated drums, and tuned snare to F and bass drum to D.

segments.title: Cowbells and temple blocks
segments.summary: His outfit included four cowbells and a set of four china or temple blocks.

segments.title: Using blocks with discipline; time on the bass drum; Mac Murray's lesson
segments.summary: Foster explains varying breaks, keeping time with the feet while the hands make 'monkeyshines', and recalls Mac Murray's advice at Lincoln Park that the bass drum makes or breaks a band.

segments.title: Drum solos: humming the melody
segments.summary: He took many solos in the old days and avoided counting bars, instead humming the melody to himself.

segments.title: Beats, breaks and rim technique on High Society
segments.summary: He demonstrates how he marks beats with his foot, makes breaks, and plays the clarinet solo in High Society using the edge of the drum.

segments.title: Stick-on-stick technique learned from Mac Murray
segments.summary: Russell describes Foster's way of striking one stick with the other to change tone, which Foster says Mac Murray also did; they compare stick sizes.

segments.title: Teaching Alec Bigard and Emile's vote for Foster
segments.summary: Foster says he tried to teach Alec Bigard the technique without success, and that Bigard's uncle Emile, a violinist, first voted him over Red Happy.

segments.title: Reel change and question on slow-blues beats
segments.summary: Tape runs out and Russell changes the reel, then asks about special beats for slow blues.

segments.title: Trumpet players' styles: Bunk, Oliver and the musical readers
segments.summary: On a second reel, Foster compares Bunk Johnson and Joe Oliver as one style with the more music-reading players such as Peter Bocage and Manuel Perez.
